Hi Russ,

Thought I might just reply to you directly on this one, at least initially.=


I used Distance 3.5 as a stand alone to do some simulation work for my =
MSc,
looking at effect of line placement in line-transect sampling (MS =
submitted
to J of Cet Res and Mgtn). I was able to successfully use VBA within Excel
to do this. Len Thomas helped significantly. It was a bit of a headache =
for
me as I had no programming experience, but it can definitely be done. I
thought about putting together something for the website that people could
download, but I was never convinced that someone else couldn't do a tidier
job of it than me, and it also seemed that the first and last sections of
the macro were fairly specific to what I was doing.

Basically, I had a large base file (Excel spreadsheet) with all my data.
This was all simulated, but based on actual data that we had gathered. =
There
were a number of 'lines' that could be selected according to some sort of
design (varying stratification and line allocation schemes, random vs
systematic), as well as a number of potential perp distances and group =
sizes
that were generated from the distributions of these that we observed on =
our
actual survey.=20

The first bit of the code simply put together an input file in the
appropriate format. There were differences in this depending on what =
design
we wanted to test. The second bit called up Distance, using a DOS window.
The tricky bit was figuring out how to get the rest of the macro that
followed *not* to run until Distance had done its thing. Len found a =
useful
bit of code for this that someone had written for Access and it worked =
very
well. Once the analysis had completed, the rest of the code simply opened
the results file and parsed the various numbers of interest to another
spreadsheet. I'll have a hunt around and find the relevant bits of the =
macro
that call up Distance and send that to you.

Cheers
Sam DuFresne

This picks up the macro once the input file has been created. I put in the =
Application.Wait command just to make sure the input file that had just =
been created had enough time to save and close. ShellWait refers to the =
code below (written by Terry Kreft). Obviously you'll have to make sure =
the path names for Distance and the input file are correct for your =
machine. The loops for MyFile were just an extra to make sure the analysis =
really had run and the files written. The results file ("Stat.txt") is =
opened and I had a messy string of code to parse the results. The problem =
was that the results files seemed to differ from time to time, depending =
on how many binnings Distance tried for the detection function. It took me =
quite a while to have enough code that it accounted for all possibilities. =
I kept thinking "there must be a better way" but couldn't think of it! =
Obviously this whole thing ran on a loop so you could specify how many =
iterations you wanted.



Application.Wait Now + TimeValue("00:00:02")

ShellWait ("C:\Program Files\Distance\D35Engine 0, C:\Temp\Comm_str.txt")

MyFile =3D Dir("C:\Temp\Log.txt")
If MyFile =3D "" Then
Do While MyFile =3D ""
Application.Wait Now + TimeValue("00:00:01")
MyFile =3D Dir("C:\Temp\Log.txt")
Loop
Else
MySize =3D FileLen("C:\Temp\Log.txt")
If MySize =3D 0 Then
Do While MySize =3D 0
Application.Wait Now + TimeValue("00:00:01")
MySize =3D FileLen("C:\Temp\Log.txt")
Loop
End If
End If

Workbooks.OpenText FileName:=3D"C:\Temp\Stat.txt", Origin:=3DxlWindows, _
startrow:=3D1, DataType:=3DxlDelimited, TextQualifier:=3DxlDoubleQu=
ote, _
ConsecutiveDelimiter:=3DTrue, Tab:=3DTrue, Semicolon:=3DFalse, =
Comma:=3DFalse, _
Space:=3DTrue, Other:=3DFalse, FieldInfo:=3DArray(Array(1, 1), =
Array(2, 1), Array(3 _
, 1), Array(4, 1), Array(5, 1), Array(6, 1), Array(7, 1), Array(8, =
1), Array(9, 1), Array(10, _

Private Const STARTF_USESHOWWINDOW& =3D &H1
Private Const NORMAL_PRIORITY_CLASS =3D &H20&
Private Const INFINITE =3D -1&

Private Type STARTUPINFO
cb As Long
lpReserved As String
lpDesktop As String
lpTitle As String
dwX As Long
dwY As Long
dwXSize As Long
dwYSize As Long
dwXCountChars As Long
dwYCountChars As Long
dwFillAttribute As Long
dwFlags As Long
wShowWindow As Integer
cbReserved2 As Integer
lpReserved2 As Long
hStdInput As Long
hStdOutput As Long
hStdError As Long
End Type
Private Type PROCESS_INFORMATION
hProcess As Long
hThread As Long
dwProcessID As Long
dwThreadID As Long
End Type
Private Declare Function WaitForSingleObject Lib "kernel32" (ByVal _
hHandle As Long, ByVal dwMilliseconds As Long) As Long
Private Declare Function CreateProcessA Lib "kernel32" (ByVal _
lpApplicationName As Long, ByVal lpCommandLine As String, ByVal _
lpProcessAttributes As Long, ByVal lpThreadAttributes As Long, _
ByVal bInheritHandles As Long, ByVal dwCreationFlags As Long, _
ByVal lpEnvironment As Long, ByVal lpCurrentDirectory As Long, _
lpStartupInfo As STARTUPINFO, lpProcessInformation As _
PROCESS_INFORMATION) As Long
Private Declare Function CloseHandle Lib "kernel32" (ByVal _
hObject As Long) As Long
Public Sub ShellWait(Pathname As String, Optional WindowStyle As Long)
Dim proc As PROCESS_INFORMATION
Dim start As STARTUPINFO
Dim ret As Long
' Initialize the STARTUPINFO structure:
With start
.cb =3D Len(start)
If Not IsMissing(WindowStyle) Then
.dwFlags =3D STARTF_USESHOWWINDOW
.wShowWindow =3D WindowStyle
End If
End With
' Start the shelled application:
ret& =3D CreateProcessA(0&, Pathname, 0&, 0&, 1&, _
NORMAL_PRIORITY_CLASS, 0&, 0&, start, proc)
' Wait for the shelled application to finish:
ret& =3D WaitForSingleObject(proc.hProcess, INFINITE)
ret& =3D CloseHandle(proc.hProcess)
End Sub

'***************** Code End ****************

Hi Russ,

I'm sending you a couple of attachments, so I hope your server is okay =
with
them (I have up-to-date Norton's definitions, so they should be safe!). =
The
PDF file is the manuscript I was telling you about. I t has been submitted
to Journal of Cetacean Research and Management (which is published by the
IWC). It should give you a fairly clear idea of what we were doing and how
(figures are attached to the end of it). I'll let you know what the status
of that is as soon as I can.

The second is the rest of the macro. Note that I have not given you the =
full
data set that we simulated, or the complete macro (I omitted some of it to
try and cut down the size, as it was originally a few MBs). The details in
the MS should explain in sufficient detail how the various data were
generated.

When you open the file you'll notice there are 2 sheets in the workbook.
"Lines" contains all the potential transect lines that can be selected.
Columns F onwards contain potential numbers of sightings for each line. In
column E, one of these is selected at random each time that "line" is
selected for a "survey". Columns A-D are stratum number, stratum area, =
line
number and line length respectively. "Dist+Group" contains group sizes and
perpendicular distances (again, a reduced set) which are also selected
randomly, but have been generated from appropriate distributions.

When you look at the macro itself, you'll notice that there are a number =
of
modules. The basic idea is as follows, on each iteration, a survey is run
using all lines ("All_lines" module). Then, subsets of these lines are
selected according to varying design principles, and the results are
compared to the results run using all lines. I have included 4 of the 8
designs that we tried to give you an idea. Like I said in my original
e-mail, I think the whole macro is a bit messy and there is probably a
better way of doing it!

What I haven't included is the Distance command file (i.e. where you tell
Distance what to estimate and how, etc...). If you're using Distance 3.5 =
as
a stand alone, you need to create a command file in the same way that we
used to do for the older DOS versions. The easiest way to do this is to
create an analysis in Distance, run it, and look at the log. There are a =
few
good tips in the Distance help files that will help explain all of that. =
(Do
a search on 'stand alone').

I'm embarrassed to say that the last time I tried to crank this macro up, =
it
didn't work. Various computer changes and hard drive crashes have resulted
in the loss of a couple of files (e.g. the command file). The macro as it =
is
will give you the basic idea, and hopefully you'll be able to put =
something
together to suit your needs.

I hope all this is helpful, and let me know if I can do anything else. I'm
certainly happy to keep corresponding with you on all of this. Best of =
luck,
and I'll look forward to hearing how you get on.

Cheers
Sam

Hi Russell,

I'm replying just to you (not the list) to give you a few leads and =
provide you=20
with the info I can -- please can you collate all the information you get =
and=20
forward it to the list at some point, so others can benefit -- thanks!

Okay, first to others who I know of - only two I'm afraid:

- Paul Luckacs at Colorado State developed some simulation software, =
WebSim, to=20
look at the optimal spacing of traps in trapping web studies. In that =
he=20
simulates data and then calls the Distance analysis engine (D4.exe) to do =
the=20
analysis. The program is written in C++ I think. You can find out more, =
and=20
contact Paul, via his web page http://www.cnr.colostate.edu/~plukacs/web.ht=
ml=20

- Tiago Marques here at St Andrews developed some quick and dirty code to =
do a=20
double platform analysis for someone in the Sea Mammal Research Unit here. =
The=20
code does a special type of bootstrap and for each bootstrap rep calls =
D4.exe to=20
do the analysis. It's written in VB. Tiago is a student here, and you =
can get=20
his email address from the Directory page of the school web site
http://www-maths.mcs.st-andrews.ac.uk/=20

Secondly, as to how you might go about it (assuming you want to/have to =
develop=20
code from scratch). =20

As you probably know, the CDS and MCDS analysis engine live in a =
separate=20
executable file D4.exe (written in FORTRAN), which is in the Distance =
program=20
directory. When you call D4.exe you pass in the location of a text file =
called=20
the command file which contains a bunch of lines of text telling distance =
what=20
analysis to do and also where a second file called the data file lives. =
The=20
data file (obviously enough) contains the data to use in that analysis, in =
"flat=20
file" format. All that happens when you press the "Run" button in =
Distance is=20
that Distance generates the appropriate files and then calls D4.exe. This =
is=20
documented in the online help on the page "Running the analysis engines as =
a=20
stand-alone program" (towards the end of Chapter 8).

Probably the best way to see what the command and data files should look =
like is=20
to get Distance to generate a template. In Distance, if you choose Tools =
|=20
Preferences and then the Analysis tab, and then tick the box "Debug mode", =
the=20
next time you run an analysis, Distance will generate the command and =
data=20
files, but will not run the analysis engine. In the Log tab of the =
Analysis=20
details, Distance will tell you where it's put the files (usually in your =
temp=20
directory) so you can have a look at them. The format of the command file =
is=20
pretty-much documented in the Distance 2.2 Users Guide, which you can =
download=20
from the Distance web site (under Distance 2.2). There have been a few =
changes:
- in batch mode (what we're using) the output files are not given in =
ASSIGN=20
statements but in the first few lines of the command file (as documented =
in the=20
online help page)
- the flat file format for the data file
- there are some new commands for MCDS analyses
The best way to get a handle on these last two is to generate some =
template=20
files as described above and see what's in them. One of these days I'll =
get=20
'round to writing an updated command manual... Meanwhile if you get =
problems=20
just drop me a line.

In many simulation applications, what you want to do is generate lots =
of=20
datasets, run the same analysis on each one, store the results, and then =
do some=20
summary statistics on the results. If you really want to run the same =
analysis=20
on each simulated dataset, then you just need to get Distance to generate =
the=20
right template command file and just use that -- otherwise your program =
will=20
have to write its own command file which can be trickier. In any case you =
will=20
have to write the data to a text file in the flat file format D4.exe =
expects --=20
you can put it where you like so long as you edit the INFILE command in =
the=20
command file. As for harvesting results, D4.exe puts out results into =
two=20
files: the results file and the stats file. The former is the long text =
file=20
that Distance displays in the Results page of the Analysis Details. The =
second=20
is a compact fixed-format summary (Distance harvests these results and =
uses them=20
to put out the summary statistics in the Analysis Browser -- but you don't =
need=20
to know that!). I suggest you use the latter as it is much easier to =
write a=20
program to parse this file. The format of the stats file is documented in =
the=20
online help on the page "Saving Results to File" (Chapter 8). You can =
also try=20
running an analysis from the command line, using the template files you've =
got=20
Distance to output, and then check out what it looks like for yourself.

Last thing is how to get your simulation program to run D4.exe. Most =
computer=20
languages have a "shell" command or some such, which allows them to run=20
programs. One problem with these is that often they start the external =
program=20
and then return control immediately to the calling routine. In your =
situation=20
you'd rather have something that waited for the analysis to finish =
before=20
returning. One solution (implemented by Tiago) is to simply have a =
"pause"=20
command and the next command after shell, causing the program to wait for =
a few=20
seconds before continuing -- in the hope that D4.exe will have finished by =
then. =20
This is simple, but a bit kludgy. A second alternative is to use Windows =
API=20
(application programming interface - a lowish-level interface to Windows) =
to do=20
it -- this takes some knowledge of how to program the Windows API. (Hint, =
if=20
you do go down this route: if you run D4.exe with CreateProcess (and =
then=20
WaitForInputIdle), you can wait for it to finish using WaitForSingleObject =
with=20
the timeout set to INFINITY.) A third way is to use the .dll which I've =
already=20
written to do the job (it's called D4CDSNEI.dll - NEI is short for =
numerical=20
engine interface). It is event driven, so you call a RunEngine method and =
then=20
wait for an event called RunFinished to fire. If you're writing in an =
event=20
driven language such as VB then that's probably the easiest way. I've put =
some=20
more information about this option at the bottom of this message, and can =
send=20
the source code if this would help.

Hope this helps to get you started -- if you have any more questions then =
give=20
me a shout. If you get desperate, I can probably do the programming (or =
at=20
least the bulk of it which you can then modify) as a short contract.

- Len

-------------------------------------------------------------------------
Using D4CDSNEI.dll

It is an ActiveX dll, so any language that talks ActiveX will be able to =
use it. =20
For example, in a Visual Basic project, you choose Project | References, =
and=20
scroll down until you see "Distance 4 CDS Numerical Engine Interface" and =
tick=20
the box by that entry. Then, if you use the VB object browser, you will =
see=20
that D4CDSNEI contains a class called CDSProcess, with methods RunEngine =
and=20
KillEngine, a property ErrMsg and an event RunFinished. I've put the=20
documentation from my code below you can see more about the class. I can =
send=20
all the code if you think it would be useful -- the rest of that .dll =
contains=20
stuff for getting settings out of a model definition and data filter and =
combing=20
them to make a command file, for putting together a data file, for =
calling=20
CDSProcess, and for parsing the results, stats and plot file to store =
results.


'-------------------------------------------------------------------------
'CDS Numerical Engine Process class - CDSProcess
'-------------------------------------------------------------------------

'Purpose: Class that represent the analysis engine process. Contains
' API routines that start the analysis and wait for it to finish. Also
' routines to stop it if necessary.

'This class is declared as public because it is not only used internally
' by CDSNEngineInterface, but it is also used in the Distance interface/
' project database for importing old D22 data.

'Interface:
' Properties:
' ErrMsg As String (read-only)
' If Status Is FileError Then
' should contain an error message giving information about
' where the error occured - this could be saved into the Log file.
' Methods:
' RunEngine (EngineFile As String,
' Infile As String, Optional ByVal Import As Boolean =3D False,
' Optional ByVal CommandLineFile As String=3D"")
' - Starts the engine run - set Import to true if you want to import
' an old distance file
' - EngineFile is the exe name -- without the path (assume the engine
' is located in App.Path)
' - CommandLineFile is a file to put command line output into if
' the engine is run under WinNT
' KillEngine - Stops a run and kills the engine process
' Events:
' RunFinished (EngineStatus As CDSEngineStatus)
' - Raised when a run has finished.=20
